A

action

An action is a functional of fields whose stationary variations give the equations of motion. Its boundary variation determines additional boundary conditions or boundary data.

Why it matters

A genuine field-theory comparison must identify the coupled actions and their variations.

Where it sits

Matching Hamiltonians at zero connection does not determine the coupling to a boundary gauge field.

Related

  • Hamiltonian
  • boundary condition
  • gauge transformation

additive normal convolution

Additive normal convolution takes the exterior tensor of two normal differential modules, pushes it forward along addition of their normal coordinates using the relative de Rham complex, and applies the declared coefficient completion.

Why it matters

It constructs a geometric product corresponding to completed derived tensor of the scalar grounds.

Where it sits

Balancing over the normal Weyl algebra instead consumes the normal coordinate and has a scalar output with a different shift.

Related

  • convolution
  • normal ground
  • de Rham differential
  • Weyl algebra

additive translation frame

An additive translation frame identifies the fibre of a formally translated object with the formal scalar extension of its original fibre, equals the identity at parameter zero, and respects addition of translation parameters.

Why it matters

It makes differentiation of translation define a coderivation on reconstructed coefficients.

Where it sits

A linear additive frame need not preserve tensor comparisons. Its tensor defect must be retained; a monoidal frame additionally intertwines the tensorators and gives a derivation of the Hopf multiplication.

Related

  • translation
  • linear fibre functor
  • tensorator
  • coend

age shift

The age is the sum of fractional normal eigenvalue angles of a finite-order action. For a surface permutation it is N−c(g)N-c(g), with c(g)c(g) its cycle count.

Why it matters

It governs the grading correction in orbifold comparison.

Where it sits

Simultaneous cochain and intrinsic-parity shifts preserve total parity and supertrace, but do not remove every field obstruction.

Related

  • orbifold sector
  • superdimension

algebraic totalization

An algebraic direct-sum totalization combines a multigraded complex by taking the direct sum of its terms in each total degree. An element therefore uses only finitely many of the summands in that degree.

Why it matters

It specifies the actual unbounded current–ghost functor and explains why an infinite telescoping primitive can be unavailable.

Where it sits

For bounded-below tail cochains, the sum and product totalizations agree degreewise. On unbounded inputs the algebraic functor has its own null system, which can be smaller than ordinary acyclicity.

Related

  • product totalization
  • cochain complex
  • null system
  • cohomology

analytification

Analytification associates a complex analytic space and analytic sheaves to an algebraic space over the complex numbers and its algebraic sheaves.

Why it matters

It permits comparison of algebraic collision coefficients with logarithmic and Dolbeault realizations.

Where it sits

Compatibility with cohomology or pushforward requires the hypotheses of the relevant algebraic–analytic comparison theorem.

Related

  • coherent sheaf
  • Dolbeault differential
  • proper map

angular form

A normalized angular form is a closed form away from a specified support whose integral around an oriented link of that support is one. Its distributional differential represents the corresponding supported source.

Why it matters

It fixes the residue and flux normalization of the brane marking.

Where it sits

The mixed two-form used here is integrated together with a holomorphic volume form. Its degree differs from the real dimension of the link.

Related

  • brane link
  • residue
  • distribution

annihilator

The annihilator of an RR-module MM is the ideal AnnR⁡(M)={r∈R:rM=0}\operatorname{Ann}_R(M)=\{r\in R:rM=0\}.

Why it matters

Annihilators distinguish the full binary shuffle cokernels and measure the exact parameter torsion of the triple image.

Where it sits

An RR-linear module isomorphism preserves its annihilator, making it an obstruction to the specified coefficient equivalences.

Related

  • torsion
  • associative algebra
  • shuffle algebra

annulus

An annulus is a region between two concentric circles, such as {z:r−<|z|<r+}\{z:r_-<|z|<r_+\} with 0<r−<r+0<r_-<r_+. It has an inner and an outer boundary.

Why it matters

An annulus separates a Laurent singularity from the compact support used to represent its residue.

Where it sits

Its two boundary orientations determine the sign in the area-to-contour comparison.

Related

  • residue
  • Laurent polynomial
  • Dolbeault differential

anomaly

An anomaly is a quantum obstruction to a required symmetry or consistency equation. In a cochain model it is a closed curvature coefficient; it can be removed in a chosen coefficient space exactly when an allowed correction supplies its primitive.

Why it matters

The cubic trace calculation decides when free holomorphic currents admit a local scalar correction.

Where it sits

The coefficient space matters: a nonzero local anomaly can become exact after nonlocal kernels or additional central fields are admitted.

Related

  • curvature
  • cohomology
  • local functional
  • propagator

antifield

An antifield is a variable conjugate to a field or ghost in the Batalin–Vilkovisky odd symplectic structure. Its degree is chosen so that the bracket has degree one.

Why it matters

Antifield terms encode the gauge transformations inside the master action.

Where it sits

Antifields are part of the cochain description and are not additional independent physical measurements.

Related

  • Batalin–Vilkovisky construction
  • BRST
  • conjugate fields

antighost

An antighost is a graded variable used in a BRST resolution of constraints, often of degree minus one. Its differential can represent a moment equation or relation among fields.

Why it matters

Antighosts retain the relations that ordinary invariants would omit.

Where it sits

The polynomial quantum example pairs antighosts with degree-one ghosts through a Clifford relation.

Related

  • ghost
  • BRST
  • Clifford algebra

antipode

The antipode of a Hopf algebra is the map 𝗌\mathsf s satisfying m(𝗌⊗1)Δ=m(1⊗𝗌)Δ=1εm(\mathsf s\otimes1)\Delta=m(1\otimes\mathsf s)\Delta=1\varepsilon. It reverses multiplication and plays the role of inversion.

Why it matters

The antipode enters the level-dependent coaction and the inverse spectral contraction. Its order is essential when the Hopf algebra is noncommutative.

Where it sits

In a twisted Hopf algebra, the antipode changes with the coproduct. Adjoining translation can alter which twists and antipodes are available.

Related

  • Hopf algebra
  • spectral form
  • coaction
  • Drinfeld twist

arithmetic interperiod comparison

An arithmetic interperiod comparison relates the actual marked operations at one period to those of the prescribed recipient at another period. It must specify its receiver, fusion junctions, tensor comparisons, regular boundary unit and duality maps.

Why it matters

It is the missing map needed to turn the positive orbit and matrix actions into the original arithmetic norm.

Where it sits

Regrouping matrices while retaining the same finest-period labels proves a different tower statement. The arithmetic tower must compare actual intermediate objects and the extra-junction tangle. Matching dimensions, loops or closed network values alone does not construct it.

Related

  • period group
  • matrix boundary action
  • regular arithmetic receiver
  • inverse reference line

associated graded

The associated graded of a filtered object is the direct sum of its successive filtration quotients. It records the leading layer of each filtration degree.

Why it matters

Finite filtrations turn bar–cobar and transfer comparisons into tractable leading-term calculations.

Where it sits

A conclusion for the associated graded requires a convergence or finite-filtration argument before it applies to the original object.

Related

  • filtration
  • cochain complex
  • spectral sequence

associative algebra

An associative algebra is a module with a bilinear multiplication satisfying (ab)c=a(bc)(ab)c=a(bc). A unit is an element 11 with 1a=a1=a1a=a1=a. A commutative algebra also satisfies ab=baab=ba, or the specified graded sign rule.

Why it matters

Associativity is the operation preserved by the duality sought in this programme.

Where it sits

An associative algebra on geometric coefficients uses a specified tensor product. Its meaning depends on that tensor and its unit.

Related

  • tensor product
  • augmentation
  • graded vector space

associative chiral algebra

An associative chiral algebra in the collision construction is an associative algebra object for the specified geometric convolution, with coherent operations on its configuration coefficients. Those coefficients and operations include collision strata, rather than only the original state space at one point.

Why it matters

It is the associative algebraic structure obtained from a field residue coalgebra by cobar and used in associative chiral duality.

Where it sits

The word-cut and collision-atlas carriers have different decompositions. Their relation requires structured restriction maps or full-overlap exchange. A Lie envelope is a special additional description.

Related

  • associative algebra
  • cobar construction
  • ordered collision atlas
  • full-overlap exchange

associator

An associator is the specified natural isomorphism between the two parenthesizations of a threefold tensor product. Its pentagon identity ensures coherent agreement among parenthesizations of longer products.

Why it matters

Its actual operator enters both hexagons when a braiding is extracted from a spectral exchange.

Where it sits

Binary comparisons for a linear fibre need not already be associative. Their transported associator must be retained until the coherence equation is solved.

Related

  • tensorator
  • hexagon identity
  • symmetric braiding
  • structural-image condition

augmentation

An augmentation of a unital algebra AA over a coefficient field kk is an algebra homomorphism ϵ:A→k\epsilon:A\to k with ϵ(1)=1\epsilon(1)=1. Its kernel is the augmentation ideal. Geometric versions use the specified tensor unit as target.

Why it matters

The augmentation ideal supplies the reduced input to a bar construction.

Where it sits

A linear expectation need not preserve multiplication. The nonzero-level Heisenberg mode algebra obstructs an augmentation although its Fock space admits constant-term evaluation.

Related

  • associative algebra
  • Heisenberg algebra
  • prepared state

automorphic line

An automorphic line is a line on a period quotient with transition action specified by a weight and, when needed, a character.

Why it matters

Modular forms are its sections.

Where it sits

The weight-five Igusa root retains a sign action. Its square can descend where the root does not descend as an ordinary coarse line.

Related

  • line bundle
  • inertia
  • Pfaffian

B

balanced tensor product

The balanced tensor product identifies the right action of an algebra on one module with its left action on the other.

Why it matters

It is the tensor product used by the arithmetic sectors over the separable extension algebra.

Where it sits

The balancing idempotent and its quotient enter the definition of their full intertwining fields.

Related

  • fusion category
  • junction

bar construction

The bar construction of an augmented associative algebra AA, with augmentation ideal aa, is the coalgebra of suspended words BA=K⊕︎⨁r≥1(sa)⋆rBA=K\oplus\bigoplus_{r\geq1}(sa)^{\star r}. Its differential combines the differential of the entries with multiplication of adjacent entries. Its coproduct cuts a word into an initial and a final segment.

Why it matters

The bar construction turns multiplication into a differential while retaining the order and geometric coefficients of the inputs.

Where it sits

For positive collision coefficients, word length is bounded by the number of labels at each configuration. The convolution and empty unit are part of the construction.

Related

  • cobar construction
  • bar–cobar duality
  • augmentation
  • coalgebra
  • isolated empty unit

bar–cobar duality

Bar–cobar duality is an equivalence between specified categories of augmented associative algebras and coaugmented coassociative coalgebras, realized by bar and cobar with comparison maps ΩBA≃A\Omega BA\simeq A and BΩC≃CB\Omega C\simeq C. It includes the structure maps and their coherent homotopies.

Why it matters

The equivalence identifies multiplication data with splitting data and supports corresponding module and interface comparisons.

Where it sits

It requires hypotheses controlling the word filtrations. The ordered collision constructions use positivity in arity. An associative algebra on the dual side additionally requires coefficient duality.

Related

  • bar construction
  • cobar construction
  • coefficient transposition
  • homotopy

Batalin–Vilkovisky algebra

A Batalin–Vilkovisky algebra is a graded-commutative algebra equipped with a square-zero operator Δ\Delta of degree one and differential-operator order at most two. Its failure to differentiate multiplication defines a degree-one bracket.

Why it matters

The contraction operator on quantum observables organizes the quantum differential, bracket and master equation.

Where it sits

The differential version includes a compatible differential. Concrete field models must specify their kernels, signs and completions.

Related

  • graded vector space
  • differential operator
  • Poisson bracket
  • quantum master equation

Batalin–Vilkovisky construction

The Batalin–Vilkovisky construction extends fields by ghosts and conjugate antifields. An odd symplectic bracket and a master action encode equations of motion, gauge symmetries and their compatibility.

Why it matters

It makes the mixed terms in a coupled gauge theory part of one differential identity.

Where it sits

A relative Batalin–Vilkovisky action can keep an external boundary differential separate from the added dynamical fields.

Related

  • antifield
  • master equation
  • symplectic form

bc ghost algebra

The bc ghost algebra has odd fields b,cb,c with conjugate first-order operator product, so b(0)cb_{(0)}c is the vacuum. In the cohomological convention here bb has degree −1 and cc has degree 1.

Why it matters

It implements the constraint differential and retains the ghost contractions that affect curvature and affine level.

Where it sits

The full bc algebra includes both fields and all modes. An exterior ghost vacuum or a commutative ghost subalgebra has a different carrier.

Related

  • ghost
  • antighost
  • operator field
  • curvature

Berezinian

The Berezinian is the even determinant tensored with the inverse odd determinant of a finite super vector bundle.

Why it matters

It is the determinant for a specified parity decomposition.

Where it sits

Exterior parity can change this line. It is not interchangeable with an independently chosen cochain determinant.

Related

  • superdimension
  • determinant line

BF theory

A BF theory pairs a field B with the curvature of a connection-like field A in its action. In a mixed holomorphic–topological version, the curvature uses the specified mixed differential and Lie bracket.

A rank-two lattice stable under a quadratic unit determines finite arithmetic period groups.

Changing the lattice can change the finite pairing, so lattice data belong to a tensor comparison.

A formal Laurent germ at zero is a series with finitely many negative powers and possibly infinitely many nonnegative powers of its parameter. It describes local punctured-coordinate data and need not have a value at zero or infinity.

Constant-log extraction can act on a polar exchange through its germ even when direct evaluation at zero is impossible.

Laurent polynomials give finite inputs on which contour residues and compact annular representatives can be compared exactly.

An LF space is a locally convex countable inductive limit of complete metrizable locally convex spaces. Smooth compactly supported tests on an exhausted manifold use the limit of smooth tests supported in its compact subsets.

A Lie algebra is a vector space with a bilinear bracket satisfying antisymmetry and the Jacobi identity. The bracket describes the commutator of infinitesimal symmetries.

An associative algebra gives a Lie algebra by taking its commutator; a Lie algebra need not come with an associative multiplication.

It gives the first-order antisymmetric coproduct that a Hopf quantization must recover.

A cone packages the precise defect of a proposed equivalence and relates the defects of composite maps through an exact triangle.

The mapping fibre is the cone shifted by minus one. Keeping that shift is essential in the boundary-coring detector.

The mapping fibre of a cochain map f is its mapping cone shifted by minus one. It is the derived object fitting into the exact triangle from the fibre to the source, then by f to the target.

The counit fibre of a relative coring produces the exact cone of the boundary endomorphism comparison after derived Hom.

observable

An observable is a quantity associated with fields in a specified region. Classically it is a function of those fields. In a quantum theory it is an element of an algebra whose product records how measurements combine.

Why it matters

Reconstruction asks which observables, products and states can be recovered from boundary data.

Where it sits

An observable can depend on a whole region. An operator field organizes observables by their insertion point.

Related

  • operator field
  • prepared state
  • correlation function

operad

An operad specifies spaces or complexes of operations with several inputs, their input symmetries, a unit, and rules for substituting operations into one another. An algebra over it is a complex on which those operations act compatibly.

Why it matters

It records which products, brackets and higher relations a field comparison must preserve.

Where it sits

An action requires actual operation maps. The existence of a trace or an abstract symmetry group does not supply them.

Related

  • colored differential graded operad
  • cochain complex
  • action

operator field

An operator field is a family of operators depending on a position. Algebraically, it is often a formal Laurent series A(z)=∑nAnz−n−1A(z)=\sum_n A_nz^{-n-1}, whose coefficients act on a vector space of states.

Why it matters

Its products retain the singular terms created when positions meet.

Where it sits

Vertex algebras specify operator fields together with a vacuum, translation and identities governing products.

Related

  • observable
  • Laurent series
  • vertex algebra

orbifold sector

An orbifold sector is the coefficient space of a group element's fixed locus, retaining twisted fields and the centralizer action.

Why it matters

Permutation sectors organize states by cycle length.

Where it sits

Identity and twisted sectors can have different charge and parity laws despite matching total indices.

Related

  • age shift
  • chiral de Rham sheaf

orbit transport

An orbit transport carries objects and junctions along an arrow of the action groupoid of a finite orbit. In the Pell construction, multiplication by the unit relabels every marked generator and fixes the coefficient scalars.

Why it matters

It constructs an actual tensor operation around an orbit, before asking for a comparison between different periods.

Where it sits

The strict functor satisfies Smm=id⁡S_m^m=\operatorname{id}, preserves both duality maps and has a graph bimodule. The covering-fibre action is affine, while its action on coefficient labels is linear. Semilinear Artin transport is a separate operation on the conjugate family.

Related

  • period group
  • graph bimodule
  • stabilizer holonomy
  • cup and cap

ordered collision atlas

The ordered collision atlas has a chart for each total order on a finite label set. Charts are glued where every pair on which their orders disagree has distinct positions. At a collision, the resulting space retains an order within each coincident block.

Why it matters

It combines exchange between separated insertions with order information at collisions.

Where it sits

Its convolution uses ordered decompositions into subsets. The word carrier uses consecutive cuts, so identifying the two requires an explicit comparison.

Related

  • configuration space
  • collision stratum
  • ordered word

ordered word

An ordered word is a finite sequence of positions. In the word carrier used here, adjacent equal entries can collapse. Nonadjacent repetitions remain: abab, abaaba and abababab are different when a≠ba\ne b.

Why it matters

The sequence retains intervening operations that a set of occupied positions would forget.

Where it sits

Consecutive cuts define its tensor product. The ordered collision atlas uses a different organization of orders and collisions.

Related

  • cut product
  • spectator
  • ordered collision atlas

orientation data

Orientation data are square-root determinant lines with specified square maps and extension compatibility.

Why it matters

They make critical coefficients and Hall maps coherent in families.

Where it sits

Strong orientation requires agreement on complete flags. Equality of line classes alone does not check square maps or signs.

Related

  • determinant line
  • vanishing cycles
  • flag

orthogonal complement

For a subgroup HH and a bicharacter χ\chi, its orthogonal complement is H⟂={g:χ(g,h)=1 for every h∈H}H^\perp=\{g:\chi(g,h)=1\text{ for every }h\in H\}.

Why it matters

The determinant of a unit-channel commutator forces a multiple of the period kernel into this complement.

Where it sits

For a perfect pairing on a finite group GG, its order is |G|/|H||G|/|H|.

Related

  • bicharacter
  • period group

p-adic valuation

For a nonzero integer nn, the pp-adic valuation vp(n)v_p(n) is the exponent of the prime pp in its factorization. It extends to nonzero rational numbers by subtraction on quotients.

Why it matters

A comparison of required and actual valuations proves that certain representation dimensions cannot occur.

Where it sits

The period obstruction compares vp(sz)v_p(sz) with the larger divisibility forced by a perfect relative pairing.

Related

  • primary subgroup
  • multiplicity space

paired vector space

A paired vector space is a vector space with a specified bilinear pairing. A nondegenerate pairing identifies the space with its linear dual. Symmetry and grading conventions are additional data.

Why it matters

Quantum contractions and sewing depend on the pairing, not only the dimension of the state space.

Where it sits

The descendant comparison uses a finite even space with a symmetric pairing and a distinguished vector.

Related

  • vector space
  • tensor product
  • cohomological field theory

parameter saturation

The parameter saturation of L⊂ML\subset M over a domain RR is the set of m∈Mm\in M for which rm∈Lrm\in L for some nonzero r∈Rr\in R.

Why it matters

It describes the multiplication image after parameter torsion is disregarded, while allowing that lost torsion to be measured separately.

Where it sits

Parameter saturation does not invert root differences. The exact integral shuffle image can be smaller than its saturated wheel ideal.

Related

  • torsion
  • annihilator
  • shuffle algebra

parity object

A parity object is an invertible object Pi whose tensor square is coherently identified with the unit, representing the odd line in a super realization. Its simple tensor products follow addition of parities modulo two.

Why it matters

Allowing the unit and a parity simple extends the internal companion construction to categories with odd current operators.

Where it sits

A coherent simple tensor skeleton does not already give a braiding on extensions. The spectral and structural-image conditions must still be checked.

Related

  • super vector space
  • simple object
  • symmetric braiding
  • structural-image condition

partition function

A partition function is a generating function or state encoding the specified correlation functions. Its variables record the insertions and other parameters. Its logarithm records connected contributions when the exponential decomposition applies.

Why it matters

Holographic reconstruction must compare the actual state and its equations, beyond local algebraic operations.

Where it sits

A formal genus expansion and a convergent thermal trace use different coefficient and analytic conventions.

Related

  • correlation function
  • prepared state
  • Gibbs state

path integral

A path integral is an integration over field histories, with weights determined by an action. A mathematical construction must specify the measure or the precise formal expansion being used.

Why it matters

It can relate bulk histories to boundary states when its domain and gluing law are controlled.

Where it sits

A Gibbs trace can be defined by operators before a corresponding path integral is established.

Related

  • action
  • Gibbs state
  • sewing

PBW basis

A Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt basis expresses an enveloping algebra in ordered monomials in a chosen basis of its Lie algebra. Odd generators use the restrictions imposed by the super relations. The associated graded algebra is the corresponding symmetric superalgebra.

Why it matters

It controls finite weight spaces, filtrations and the coefficient domains used in completion.

Where it sits

An analogous basis for a quotient or quantum algebra requires its own presentation and proof.

Related

  • enveloping algebra
  • filtration
  • associated graded
  • super vector space

PBW filtration

The PBW filtration filters an enveloping algebra by the number of Lie generators in a product. Its associated graded is the symmetric algebra in the same coefficient tensor. For a positive collision Lie object, the weight at a configuration II is at most |I||I|.

Why it matters

It separates primitive outputs from products at several positions and gives detectors for centre classes and evaluation obstructions.

Where it sits

Symmetrization provides an equivariant projection to degree one in the characteristic construction. Higher PBW outputs of an arbitrary actor map require a homotopy before this projection can be used in a naturality argument.

Related

  • enveloping algebra
  • characteristic map
  • primitive-compatible comparison
  • positive configuration support

Pell equation

A Pell equation is an equation x2−dy2=1x^2-dy^2=1 with integer unknowns and a fixed positive nonsquare integer dd. Its positive solutions correspond to norm-one quadratic units.

Why it matters

Powers of 2+32+\sqrt3 give an infinite family of fusion multiplicities and tensor-lift obstructions.

Where it sits

The Pell family is one arithmetic domain inside the broader real quadratic period problem.

Related

  • real quadratic field
  • norm-one unit

perfect complex

A perfect complex over a ring is a complex equivalent to a retract of a bounded complex of finite-rank free modules. For sheaves, this condition is imposed locally. Such complexes admit finite projective duality and are compact in the derived category of modules.

Why it matters

Perfectness makes evaluation and coevaluation finite and underlies the stages used in pro-perfect coefficient duality.

Where it sits

Perfectness over differential operators and perfectness over the function ring are different conditions. Full coefficient transposition uses the former; diagonal-tensor dualizability uses the latter after normalization.

Related

  • pro-perfect coefficient
  • dualizable object
  • coefficient transposition
  • differential operator

period group

For a lattice II preserved by a norm-one unit ee, the period group is Gj=(ej−1)−1I/IG_j=(e^j-1)^{-1}I/I. Its order is ej+e−j−2e^j+e^{-j}-2.

Why it matters

It labels the invertible simple objects in the arithmetic fusion category at period jj.

Where it sits

Multiplication by (er−1)/(e−1)(e^r-1)/(e-1) gives the period quotient Gr→G1G_r\to G_1.

Related

  • lattice
  • norm-one unit
  • bicharacter

period map

A period map records the variation of Hodge subspaces of geometric cohomology, with its marking and polarization.

Why it matters

It relates an independently defined family to a period domain.

Where it sits

A lattice identity alone does not construct this map. Lines and sections also require their stabilizer actions.

Related

  • Hodge structure
  • Siegel upper half-space
  • automorphic line

periodization

Periodization adjoins an invertible class of positive homotopy degree, making its multiplication an equivalence of shifted modules.

Why it matters

It matches an ordinary complex with an even-periodic elliptic residue coefficient.

Where it sits

A nonzero bounded complex cannot remain literally unchanged as a module over that periodic ring. Completion and periodization need their own comparison.

Related

  • ring spectrum
  • spectral elliptic coefficient

Pfaffian

The Pfaffian of an alternating matrix is the signed polynomial whose square is its determinant. In families it lies in a specified square-root line.

Why it matters

It retains a sign character that squaring can forget.

Where it sits

The two-by-two skew block with entry uu has Pfaffian uu. Geometric comparison needs the skew complex, orientation and section normalization.

Related

  • determinant line
  • orientation data
  • automorphic line

Poincaré line bundle

The Poincaré line bundle is the universal degree-zero line on an elliptic curve times its dual, normalized on the zero sections.

Why it matters

It retains both period transitions in Fourier–Mukai families.

Where it sits

Its base factors and Chern class enter critical coefficients. Deleting a translated factor can change the differential.

Related

  • elliptic curve
  • line bundle
  • Fourier–Mukai transform

pointed action

A pointed action on a coalgebra CC is a map F⊗!C→CF\otimes^!C\to C whose restriction along the specified local vacuum J→FJ\to F is the identity of CC, with that identification retained as part of the derived data.

Why it matters

The pointing says that the actor vacuum acts as the identity and determines the relative source used by characteristic naturality.

Where it sits

A pointing does not supply an augmentation F→JF\to J. It also does not by itself equip FF with a coherent transverse monoid multiplication.

Related

  • transverse monoid
  • scalar-current object
  • characteristic map
  • coherent-action object

Poisson bracket

A Poisson bracket is a Lie bracket on an algebra that differentiates multiplication in each argument. In coordinates q,pq,p with {q,p}=1\{q,p\}=1, it is {f,g}=fqgp−fpgq\{f,g\}=f_qg_p-f_pg_q. Graded brackets include the corresponding degree signs.

Why it matters

It turns functions into Hamiltonian symmetries and tests whether boundary charges preserve the bulk symmetry algebra.

Where it sits

A symplectic form determines a Poisson bracket. The degrees of bulk, boundary and support-loop brackets must be tracked separately.

Related

  • Lie algebra
  • symplectic form
  • commutator

Poisson cohomology

Poisson cohomology is the cohomology of polyvector fields with differential dπ=[π,−]d_\pi=[\pi,-], where π\pi is a Poisson bivector and the bracket is the Schouten bracket. The equation [π,π]=0[\pi,\pi]=0 makes this differential square zero.

Why it matters

It gives the differential matching the regraded Chevalley–Eilenberg coordinates.

Where it sits

For nonzero π it differs from the zero differential in ordinary polynomial HKR.

Related

  • polyvector
  • Schouten bracket
  • Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg map

polarization

A polarization splits a symplectic space into two complementary isotropic subspaces, usually interpreted as creation and annihilation directions. In the Laurent model, positive and negative powers give the chosen split.

Why it matters

A Fock vacuum is defined by the annihilation subspace, so a state comparison must preserve the required polarization.

Where it sits

A symplectic map can exchange the two subspaces and therefore fail to preserve the chosen vacuum.

Related

  • symplectic form
  • Fock space
  • vacuum

polynomial

A polynomial is a finite sum of monomials in variables with coefficients in a specified ring. Even when infinitely many variables are available, each polynomial uses only finitely many of them and has finite degree.

Why it matters

Polynomial state spaces make every Wick contraction sum finite on fixed inputs.

Where it sits

A formal completion admits infinite coefficient sequences under a stated filtration. Passing to it can change continuity and duality.

Related

  • formal power series
  • Fock space
  • contraction

polyvector

A polyvector is an exterior product of vector fields, or a section of the corresponding exterior power of the tangent bundle. Functions are polyvectors of exterior degree zero.

Why it matters

Polyvectors describe Hochschild cohomology on a smooth commutative affine algebra.

Where it sits

Their exterior product and Schouten bracket model two different Hochschild operations.

Related

  • tangent complex
  • Schouten bracket
  • Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg map

positive configuration support

A coefficient system has positive configuration support when its coefficient at the empty configuration is zero. Every nonzero factor in a disjoint convolution must then occupy a nonempty set of labels.

Why it matters

At a configuration of n labels, a convolution word with more than n positive factors vanishes. This makes the normalized bar and cobar filtrations finite there.

Where it sits

This is a support condition in the number of labels, not a bound on the cohomological degrees of a coefficient complex.

Related

  • isolated empty unit
  • bar–cobar duality
  • configuration space
  • cochain complex

prefactorization algebra

A prefactorization algebra assigns observables to open sets and gives compatible operations that combine observables from finitely many disjoint open sets inside a larger one. These operations include a unit and satisfy the prescribed symmetry and nesting identities.

Why it matters

Disjoint Wick operations construct such a structure on the minimal enlargement of the current algebra.

Where it sits

A factorization algebra additionally satisfies the relevant local gluing condition. Closure under disjoint products alone supplies the prefactorization structure.

Related

  • factorization
  • observable
  • Wick contraction

prepared state

A prepared state is a specified evaluation of observables arising from physical or geometric boundary data. On an observable algebra it is represented by a linear functional. In a positive quantum theory it is normalized and satisfies λ(a∗a)≥0\lambda(a^*a)\geq0 on its stated domain.

Why it matters

It turns an algebra of operations into numerical correlation functions.

Where it sits

A vacuum vector, an integration cycle, a thermal trace and a scalar augmentation impose different data and compatibility conditions.

Related

  • observable
  • vacuum
  • correlation function
  • augmentation

preprojective algebra

A preprojective algebra is the path algebra of a doubled quiver modulo the vertex relations equating the sum of forward–reverse compositions with the sum of reverse–forward compositions, with the chosen orientation signs.

Why it matters

Its nilpotent modules model finite extensions of the specified stable K3 line bundles.

Where it sits

The completed algebra uses the arrow-ideal topology. The Hall algebras in the construction still use an algebraic direct sum over charges.

Related

  • quiver
  • nilpotent module
  • Hall algebra

primary subgroup

The pp-primary subgroup of a finite abelian group consists of elements annihilated by some power of the prime pp. The group is the direct sum of these subgroups over its prime divisors.

Why it matters

Prime-by-prime representation dimensions isolate the arithmetic obstruction at a common odd prime.

Where it sits

The subgroup for p=2p=2 can require quadratic corrections unavailable at odd primes.

Related

  • p-adic valuation
  • projective representation

prime power

A prime power is an integer prp^r with pp prime and r≥1r\ge1.

Why it matters

Every such integer contributes to the full arithmetic explicit formula.

Where it sits

The von Mangoldt weight is Λ(pr)=log⁡p\Lambda(p^r)=\log p, not log⁡(pr)\log(p^r).

Related

  • Weil form

primitive curve class

A primitive curve class is an integral homology class that is not a multiple greater than one of another integral class.

Why it matters

Primitive reduced counts give the monic inverse Igusa identity.

Where it sits

Imprimitive counts use a separate multiple-cover theorem. This notion differs from a primitive Hopf element.

Related

  • reduced Donaldson–Thomas invariant

primitive element

A primitive element xx of a coalgebra with unit satisfies Δx=x⊗1+1⊗x\Delta x=x\otimes1+1\otimes x. Its reduced coproduct is zero.

Why it matters

Charge preservation and the specified two-sided counit force charge-one shuffle currents to be primitive, producing the ordinary cooperation obstruction.

Where it sits

A cochain primitive is a different usage: it is an element whose differential is a given cocycle. Spectral coproducts can also have translated counit formulas.

Related

  • tensor product
  • cochain complex

primitive-compatible comparison

A primitive-compatible comparison is a tensor equivalence whose induced envelope map preserves the inclusion of Lie generators and the equivariant PBW-degree-one projection, together with the vacuum, partition and collision coherences.

Why it matters

The canonical family built from factorization coefficients supplies the tensor data needed for characteristic naturality under arbitrary pointed actor arrows.

Where it sits

Its theorem includes unbounded actors and full derived section tests. Singleton normalization alone does not establish this comparison for independently chosen admissibility equivalences. A sign twist of arbitrary comparison data can change the characteristic values while leaving raw actor tests unchanged.

Related

  • tensorator
  • PBW filtration
  • characteristic map

principal part

The principal part of a meromorphic expression along a divisor is its polar class modulo regular expressions. If the divisor has equation u=0u=0, its algebraic coefficient module is A[u−1]/AA[u^{-1}]/A, generated by the classes of negative powers of uu.

Why it matters

Principal parts retain the supported collision contributions from which residues and normal-transfer maps are built.

Where it sits

Taking the residue extracts one coefficient of a principal part. Keeping only that scalar coefficient can lose the higher normal modes and their differential-operator relations.

Related

  • residue

pro-perfect coefficient

A pro-perfect coefficient is an inverse diagram of perfect complexes, regarded as an object of their pro-category. The diagram and its transition maps are retained. If a differential module is presented as M=colimα⁡PαM=\operatorname{colim}_\alpha P_\alpha with perfect stages, its coefficient dual is the inverse diagram {Pα†}α\{P_\alpha^\dagger\}_\alpha.

Why it matters

This recipient retains full current coefficients that are not holonomic while allowing finite projective duality at each stage.

Where it sits

A pro-object is not generally determined by its ordinary inverse limit. A nonzero inverse diagram can have zero ordinary limit; its mapping spaces still retain the diagram.

Related

  • perfect complex

product totalization

A product totalization combines a multigraded complex by taking a product over the terms of each total degree. It permits infinitely many nonzero components in that degree, subject to the stated coefficient conditions.

Why it matters

For current tail cochains, recursive primitives in exterior degree are legal in this product, so acyclic inputs remain acyclic.

Where it sits

Each exterior-degree component still has finite algebraic mode support. This change can create extra recovery classes and obstruct extension of the old evaluation; it does not itself prove an unbounded equivalence.

  • algebraic totalization

projective bornological tensor

The projective bornological tensor product represents bounded bilinear maps from two bornological vector spaces. Its separated completion gives the complete projective bornological tensor used for the supported test and coefficient spaces.

Why it matters

It fixes the recipient in which the geometric kernels and formal coefficient operations are continuous.

Where it sits

Completing a tensor product is additional data; it is not interchangeable with an arbitrary product of field or word coefficients.

Related

  • bornology

projective representation

A projective representation assigns invertible operators AgA_g with AgAh=c(g,h)AghA_gA_h=c(g,h)A_{gh} for a scalar cocycle cc. An ordinary representation has c=1c=1.

Why it matters

The dimensions of projective blocks constrain the available multiplicity spaces of a proposed tensor lift.

Where it sits

Reciprocal projective actions combine through a prescribed bicharacter.

Related

  • scalar cocycle
  • multiplicity space

propagator

A propagator is a specified integral kernel implementing a homotopy inverse or partial inverse for the free field differential. In heat regularization it integrates a gauge-fixing operator against heat kernels over a declared scale interval.

Why it matters

Its contractions construct Wick products, higher corrections and nonlocal primitives.

Where it sits

Support, singularities, endpoint scales and signs determine its domain. Reflected and mixed matrix entries can contribute even when individual diagonal contractions agree.

Related

  • integral kernel
  • heat kernel
  • homotopy
  • Wick contraction

proper map

A proper map in algebraic geometry is separated, of finite type and universally closed. For the complex geometric spaces used here, properness ensures that compact-support transfer behaves as required over the target.

Why it matters

Invariant flags form closed loci in projective flag bundles, so forgetting flags gives proper Hall correspondences.

Where it sits

Support proper over each target open is also the support condition in the exceptional pushforward. It does not impose finite order on coefficient duals.

Related

  • flag

Prym part

The Prym part is the anti-invariant first cohomology of a double cover under its deck involution.

Why it matters

It carries cover variation absent from invariant base cohomology.

Where it sits

For the genus-two cover branched at two elliptic points it has rational dimension two. Its integral pairing and gluing remain additional data.

Related

  • elliptic curve
  • local system

quantum determinant

A quantum determinant is the determinant adapted to a matrix quantum-group relation, with ordered entries and spectral shifts. For a rank-two creation matrix, one convention is Q(u)=L11(u)L22(u−ℏ)−L21(u)L12(u−ℏ)Q(u)=L_{11}(u)L_{22}(u-\hbar)-L_{21}(u)L_{12}(u-\hbar). Its coefficients are central in the corresponding unextended double Yangian.

Why it matters

Different coproduct shifts of these central coefficients obstruct a comparison by inner conjugation.

Where it sits

Imposing determinant one removes this particular central witness. Adjoining translation changes centrality because translation differentiates the determinant series.

Related

  • double Yangian
  • Drinfeld twist

quantum group

A quantum group in the Hopf-algebra sense is an algebra with compatible product, coproduct, counit and antipode, often obtained by deforming an enveloping algebra. A formal quantization specifies its reduction and the first antisymmetric term of its coproduct.

Why it matters

It packages the multiplication and tensor symmetries sought in the chiral and geometric constructions.

Where it sits

A universal R-matrix, an automorphic realization and a physical representation category are additional structures or comparisons.

Related

  • Hopf algebra

  • universal R-matrix

quantum master equation

The quantum master equation for an interaction II is DI+12{I,I}=0DI+\tfrac12\{I,I\}=0, where DD includes the free differential and quantum contraction. It expresses compatibility of the interaction with the quantized symmetry structure.

Why it matters

Bulk–boundary couplings must solve this scalar equation, including terms invisible to the associated Hamiltonian vector field.

Where it sits

Its precise degrees depend on the shifted convention. In an unquantized even boundary phase space the analogous scalar master equation has an odd Hamiltonian.

  • Batalin–Vilkovisky algebra

quantum vertex algebra

A quantum vertex algebra is a field algebra with vacuum and translation whose opposite ordered products are compared by a specified operator 𝒮(z)\mathcal S(z). The exchange obeys the Yang–Baxter equation, compatibility with products, and the stated inversion and translation identities. The coefficient ring, completion and allowed poles belong to the definition.

Why it matters

It describes field products whose exchange depends nontrivially on separation.

Where it sits

The rational examples use exchange poles only at coincident positions. Trigonometric or dynamical exchanges require their own domains.

  • vertex algebra

quartet resolution

A quartet resolution adjoins two even and two odd free fields in differential pairs to the boundary vertex algebra. In the Heisenberg construction the differential sends tt to η\eta and ι\iota to pp, while the boundary current is represented by J+pJ+p.

Why it matters

It realizes the ghost action by a roof of vertex-algebra maps and constructs a coherent transverse monoid through a tower of compatible resolutions.

Where it sits

The ghost maps to −η-\eta, with primitive −t-t, fixing its positive characteristic class. The resulting moving-vacuum singleton is universal for a module problem; the transverse monoid is not a final factorizing actor.

quasi-coherent module

A quasi-coherent sheaf is locally the sheaf associated with a module over the coordinate ring of an affine open set. A quasi-coherent differential module additionally has the specified compatible action of differential operators.

Why it matters

It identifies the ordinary recipient in which the full auxiliary extraordinary integral is tested for existence.

Where it sits

A free differential-module summand need not be holonomic. Existence results for holonomic coefficients do not automatically extend to every quasi-coherent differential module.

  • differential module

quasi-isomorphism

A quasi-isomorphism is a cochain map inducing an isomorphism in every cohomological degree. Derived categories invert these maps, using the chosen class of complexes and allowed morphisms.

Why it matters

It permits a resolution or smaller complex to represent the same derived object.

Where it sits

A quasi-isomorphism of underlying complexes may fail to preserve an algebra action or a geometric support condition.

Related

  • cochain complex
  • cohomology
  • derived tensor product

quiver

A quiver is a directed graph. A representation assigns a vector space to each vertex and a linear map to each arrow; relations impose equations on compositions along paths.

Why it matters

Extension spaces between geometric objects give explicit quiver models for their deformation and Hall problems.

Where it sits

Doubling a quiver adds a reverse arrow for each arrow. The preprojective relations then impose a moment equation at every vertex.

  • vector space
  • preprojective algebra

quotient

A quotient identifies objects or elements according to a specified relation. For a module and a submodule, it identifies two elements when their difference lies in the submodule.

Why it matters

Quotients encode collision relations and determine which classes remain in a state space.

Where it sits

A derived quotient can retain homotopy information lost by an ordinary quotient.

Related

radical of a finite algebra

The radical of a finite-dimensional commutative algebra is its ideal of nilpotent elements, equivalently the intersection of its maximal ideals. Some finite power of this ideal is zero, and the quotient is a product of residue fields.

Why it matters

Nilpotence makes logarithms and exponentials in the structural-image and Laurent-normalization constructions finite in their radical parts.

Where it sits

The radical need not be the entire algebra. Nonzero residue constants and integer valuations must be retained separately in the factorization of a Laurent unit.

Related

  • residue valuation
  • Laurent germ
  • structural-image condition
  • idempotent

radical of a pairing

The radical of a bicharacter consists of the elements that pair trivially with every element of the group. A pairing is nondegenerate exactly when its radical is zero.

Why it matters

The radical determines the central types and block sizes of the relevant twisted group algebra.

Where it sits

For the doubled kernel action, the pairing is an alternating commutator form on two copies of a finite group.

Related

  • bicharacter
  • twisted group algebra

Ran space

The Ran space of a space X parametrizes nonempty finite subsets of X. Its coordinate charts use finite powers of X, with diagonal maps identifying repeated labels. The cardinality can vary, and no total order is chosen on the subset.

Why it matters

It provides the geometric carrier for chiral Lie–coalgebra duality and factorization structures on unordered finite configurations.

Where it sits

Pulling a Ran object to ordered charts and adjoining an empty coefficient are specified operations. Recovering a Ran object from ordered data requires coherent collision descent.

Related

  • configuration space
  • factorization
  • ordered collision atlas
  • descent

rational mode action

A rational mode action arises from a coaction of the specified mode coalgebra. In the junction example, sufficiently high regular odd modes annihilate each vector.

Why it matters

It retains finite mode support for each state while allowing infinitely many available modes.

Where it sits

The coalgebra and its topology determine the meaning of rationality.

Related

  • operator field
  • semiderived category

real quadratic field

A real quadratic field is a field ℚ(d)\mathbb Q(\sqrt d), where d>0d>0 is a nonsquare integer. It has two real embeddings, which send d\sqrt d to opposite signs.

Why it matters

Its units and lattices determine the period groups and arithmetic coefficients used in the fusion constructions.

Where it sits

The examples use ℚ(3)\mathbb Q(\sqrt3) and ℚ(5)\mathbb Q(\sqrt5).

Related

  • lattice
  • norm-one unit

A square-zero extension R⊕︎MR\oplus M has product (r,m)(s,n)=(rs,rn+sm)(r,m)(s,n)=(rs,rn+sm), so two inputs from MM multiply to zero.

Why it matters

It gives an independently constructed algebra whose bar can be computed with all cuts.

Its existence uses the module MM; it does not assume a multiplication on a module quotient such as (R/2)/c4(R/2)/c_4.

stabilizer

The stabilizer of a point under a group action is the subgroup of elements that fix that point.

Why it matters

It determines whether a transitive action on quantizations or cyclic gauge classes is free and hence a torsor.

Where it sits

Adding a parity involution can create a two-element stabilizer on a previously free single orbit.

  • action

The stabilizer holonomy of an equivariant object on a length-mm orbit is the composite H:SmmX→XH:S_m^mX\to X around the orbit. When Smm=1S_m^m=1, it is an automorphism of XX.

It retains the action of group elements that return to the same orbit vertex.

For the original integer action, HH is arbitrary. In the specified C4C_4 quotient, H4/m=1H^{4/m}=1; a two-cycle still permits H=−1H=-1. Setting every holonomy to one changes the equivariant domain.

stable marked curve

A stable marked curve is a connected nodal algebraic curve with distinct smooth marked points and a finite automorphism group. Each rational component needs at least three special points, and each genus-one component needs at least one.

Why it matters

Stability gives the compact moduli spaces used for descendant and sewing classes.

For a smooth curve with genus gg and nn markings, stability requires 2g−2+n>02g-2+n>0.

Related

stable pair

A stable pair is a map 𝒪X→F\mathcal O_X\to F with FF a pure one-dimensional coherent sheaf and zero-dimensional cokernel.

Why it matters

It supplies a sheaf model for curve counts with point contributions.

Where it sits

Purity excludes nonzero zero-dimensional subsheaves. Curve class and Euler characteristic are specified.

Related

  • coherent sheaf

stable-weight completion

The stable-weight completion consists of formal sums of monomials with weight k=2b+n≥0k=2b+n\ge0 and descendant bound ∑j(2dj+1)≤3k\sum_j(2d_j+1)\le3k. Each fixed-weight coefficient is finite-dimensional.

These bounds make the full quantum descendant operator and its inverse exponential well-defined.

The negative-mode presentation also retains k−nk-n even and is an algebra over K[[λ2]]K[[\lambda^2]].

standard current–ghost kernel

A standard current–ghost kernel TpT_p is the ghost transform of the smooth Heisenberg module generated by a vector killed by every current mode of index at least pp. Mode-linear maps from TpT_p form its probe complex.

Why it matters

The family of probe complexes defines which curved-module maps become equivalences and supplies the recovery functor by a filtered union.

These probes determine a particular localization. Its null objects include the ordinary ghost vacuum, so it is not automatically the localization appropriate to a different vacuum-preserving theory.

state augmentation

A state augmentation is a specified unital map from a state algebra to the scalar state algebra, compatible with the differential and the field structure under consideration. It sends the local vacuum to one.

Why it matters

Applied to every state decoration of a word coefficient, it gives a retraction of the scalar vacuum inclusion while retaining the positive word, its density and normal derivatives.

Projection through the isolated empty coefficient instead kills every positive word. A coring counit also does not automatically provide a scalar differential graded algebra augmentation.

strong tensor functor

A strong tensor functor preserves tensor products and the tensor unit through specified invertible comparison maps. These maps must satisfy the associativity and unit coherence equations.

Why it matters

It is the structure required to lift a positive fusion-ring map to a categorical comparison.

Where it sits

A functor can preserve object multiplicities while failing these coherence equations.

  • tensorator

structural-image condition

The structural-image conditions test whether the reference flip and spectral coefficients lift to actual internal morphisms, and whether all required placements of those coefficients, associators and translation tensorators lie in common finite commutative local algebras with the prescribed identity residues.

Why it matters

They make constant-log extraction an internal symmetric braiding that preserves the original associator and formal translations.

Where it sits

The conditions concern specified structural operations. They do not require all extension operators to commute or hold automatically for every Laurent presentation.

Sugawara state

The quadratic Sugawara state is one half of the invariant quadratic combination of affine currents, using the inverse invariant form and the ordered vertex product. It is defined before division by the level-dependent normalization.

Why it matters

Its mode relations supply translation and weight homotopies, and its critical class is a concrete input to the level Bockstein.

Where it sits

Keeping the quadratic numerator permits statements at critical values where the usual normalized conformal-vector expression has a zero denominator.

super vector space

A super vector space is a vector space split into even and odd parts. Interchanging homogeneous vectors contributes a minus sign exactly when both are odd. An even map preserves parity, while an odd map reverses it.

Why it matters

Odd current operators can produce even two-factor spectral corrections with poles, although the category’s morphisms remain even.

Where it sits

Parity signs are distinct from the choice of an internal morphism. The odd coefficients on a super fibre need not themselves be ordinary morphisms of the original category.

Related

  • parity object

  • symmetric braiding

superconnection

A superconnection is a degree-one operator on a graded family of modules that combines an internal differential, a connection and higher differential-form components. Its square is its curvature.

Why it matters

The supported boundary construction packages an action and its two explicit equivariance homotopies into one square-zero operator.

Where it sits

A flat superconnection gives all component compatibility equations simultaneously; each component’s degree and sign remain part of the definition.

Related

  • curvature
  • cochain complex
  • equivariance

superdimension

The superdimension is even dimension minus odd dimension.

Why it matters

It is the numerical information retained by many protected indices.

Where it sits

The spaces 1|651|65 and 29|9329|93 have the same value −64-64. That equality does not identify their parity spaces.

Related

  • Euler characteristic
  • elliptic genus

supersingular point

A supersingular point of elliptic moduli is a positive-characteristic elliptic curve whose formal group has height two.

Why it matters

It detects integral coefficients invisible on complex and ordinary cusp charts.

Where it sits

The displayed characteristic-two coefficient retains 𝔽4[[z]]/(z4)\mathbb F_4[[z]]/(z^4), including four infinitesimal layers.

Related

  • spectral elliptic coefficient
  • torsion

supertrace

The supertrace of an endomorphism of a finite graded vector space is the trace on its even part minus the trace on its odd part. It vanishes on graded commutators.

Why it matters

It normalizes the cyclic matrix class and detects why the raw identity vanishes in a balanced example.

Where it sits

The supertrace of the identity is the even dimension minus the odd dimension.

Related

  • graded vector space
  • commutator
  • negative-cyclic complex

symmetric braiding

A symmetric braiding is a natural invertible exchange of the two factors of a tensor product which satisfies both hexagon identities with the category's associator and whose double exchange is the identity.

Why it matters

An auxiliary symmetric braiding preserved by translation supplies the symmetric fibre used in Laurent normalization.

Where it sits

A natural internal involution can still fail a hexagon. The auxiliary braiding is not required to be a specialization of the spectral symmetry.

Related

  • hexagon identity

  • spectral symmetry

symplectic form

A symplectic form is a closed, nondegenerate two-form. It identifies covectors with vectors and thereby assigns a Hamiltonian vector field to a function. Graded versions can have even or odd degree.

Why it matters

The symplectic form fixes the signs and degrees of the physical brackets.

Where it sits

On a graded space, the form has a specified degree, which fixes the degree and signs of its Poisson bracket. Boundary potentials and endpoint charges must use compatible conventions.

Related

  • Hamiltonian
  • conjugate fields
  • Poisson bracket
  • Batalin–Vilkovisky construction

symplectic loop

A symplectic loop on a paired vector space is an invertible formal series R(z)R(z) satisfying R(−z)∗R(z)=1R(-z)^*R(z)=1. Its logarithm has coefficients rℓ∗=(−1)ℓ+1rℓr_\ell^*=(-1)^{\ell+1}r_\ell.

This identity makes the loop compatible with the residue pairing used in quantization.

Where it sits

A unit-preserving loop also fixes the distinguished unit vector in the required sense.

Related

  • paired vector space

T

tangent complex

A tangent complex is the derived replacement for a tangent space. Its degrees retain infinitesimal deformations, their symmetries and their obstruction equations.

Why it matters

It determines the degree and nondegeneracy of a shifted symplectic comparison.

Where it sits

A tangent triangle for a derived intersection need not split into a direct sum.

Related

  • cochain complex
  • shifted symplectic structure

Tate curve

A Tate curve is an elliptic curve presented by multiplicative uniformization. Over the complex numbers, a parameter q with 0 < |q| < 1 gives the quotient of the nonzero complex numbers by multiplication by powers of q. A corresponding formal construction uses the parameter q.

Why it matters

It supplies the elliptic curve whose cover states and coefficient algebras are compared.

Where it sits

The parameter, cover and relative dualizing line must be retained in the state construction.

Related

  • elliptic curve

tensor product

The tensor product V⊗RWV\otimes_R W represents bilinear maps that balance the two actions of a commutative ring RR. Its elements are finite sums of elementary tensors unless a topology and completion are specified. A monoidal category has its own tensor operation, associativity maps and unit.

Why it matters

It combines independent states or coefficient systems before operations act.

Where it sits

Ordinary, derived, completed, cut and braided tensor products preserve different information. Their comparison is part of the mathematics.

Related

  • vector space
  • derived tensor product
  • cut product

tensorator

A tensorator is the specified product comparison of a monoidal functor, typically a map F(X)⊗F(Y)→F(X⊗Y)F(X)\otimes F(Y)\to F(X\otimes Y), compatible with associativity and units. A strong monoidal functor has invertible tensorators and unit comparison.

Why it matters

It identifies the actual products on two sides of a duality, rather than only their underlying objects.

For spectral fields, cross contractions determine the tensorator. Its three-factor coherence, vacuum behavior, and extension across collisions must be checked on the chosen coefficients.

  • tensor product

test field

A test field is a field in a specified space on which distributions or observable functionals can be evaluated. Smooth compactly supported fields and Schwartz fields are common choices.

Why it matters

The test space determines which kernels, derivatives and integrals define valid observables.

Where it sits

Boundary conditions impose additional restrictions on the allowed test fields.

  • Schwartz field

thick subcategory

The thick subcategory generated by P is the smallest full subcategory containing P and closed under finite cones, shifts and retracts. It contains the finite derived constructions that can be built from P.

Why it matters

It gives the precise boundary-generated sector equivalent to perfect modules over the boundary endomorphism algebra.

Recovering all modules additionally requires a compact generator and compatibility with arbitrary coproducts.

Thom class

A Thom class is an oriented cohomology class in the normal direction of an embedding or vector bundle. It identifies coefficients on the base with coefficients supported in the normal bundle, with a degree shift equal to the real rank.

Why it matters

Complex Thom classes normalize the critical graph and the contributions of both branches of the nodal coefficient.

A complex line has real rank two. Its positive complex orientation fixes the signs used with compact trace.

Thom–Whitney totalization

A Thom–Whitney totalization combines complexes assigned to multiple overlaps by tensoring them with polynomial differential forms on simplices and requiring equality on every face.

Why it matters

It keeps local deformation equations and their overlap compatibilities in a single carrier while preserving the bracket and tensor signs.

Its completed form takes the inverse limit in a declared filtration. Completeness and the face-extension property are used in the obstruction theorem.

The Todd class is the characteristic class with factor x/(1−e−x)x/(1-e^{-x}) for each Chern root xx of a complex vector bundle. It appears in Riemann–Roch formulas.

Why it matters

Its square root corrects the pairing in the Hochschild-to-Hodge state comparison.

On a quartic K3 surface, the Todd class is 1+2p1+2p, and its square root is 1+p1+p.

Tor group

A Tor group is the homology in a specified degree of a derived tensor product. It records the failure of ordinary tensor product to be exact; it can be computed by resolving one input by flat or projective modules.

It retains the extra fibre and fusion classes that ordinary coefficient substitution can lose.

Where it sits

Flatness over the scalar ring does not imply flatness over an algebra through which two modules are balanced.

torsion

Over a domain RR, an element of a module is torsion if some nonzero element of RR annihilates it. For a specified ideal, ideal-torsion instead means that some power of that ideal annihilates the element.

Parameter torsion retains integral collision information, while ideal-torsion characterizes the finite-normal coefficient objects.

These meanings specify different coefficient conditions. Neither is automatically the same as topological support on a closed set.

torsor

A torsor for a group is a space locally carrying a free transitive group action, without a chosen identity point.

It lets extension endpoints live on one common elliptic curve.

A product over the classifying stack retains the identification of their torsors.

trace-class operator

A trace-class operator is an operator on a Hilbert space whose singular values have finite sum. Its trace is well-defined and independent of the orthonormal basis.

Why it matters

The heat operator must be trace class for the thermal partition function to be finite.

Trace-class control is an analytic condition beyond formal Hamiltonian expressions. Local nuclearity or square summability alone does not establish it on the stated Hilbert space.

translation

Translation in a field algebra is an operator TT with T𝟏=0T\mathbf1=0 and [T,Y(a,z)]=Y(Ta,z)=∂zY(a,z)[T,Y(a,z)]=Y(Ta,z)=\partial_zY(a,z). It expresses how changing the insertion point acts on states.

Holomorphic translation is distinct from evolution along an additional real direction. Comparing them requires a specified homotopy or physical construction.

A transported convolution is the product obtained by carrying a geometric convolution through a specified equivalence. It gives the product for which the transpose of bar deconcatenation is an associative algebra multiplication.

A product with the same underlying coefficients need not be this transported product. Comparing it with a field tensor requires an explicit coherent product comparison.

transverse monoid

A transverse monoid is an associative algebra object among connected coaugmented collision coalgebras equipped with the diagonal tensor ⊗!\otimes^!. Its multiplication is a coalgebra map F⊗!F→FF\otimes^!F\to F, and its unit is a coalgebra map J→FJ\to F, where JJ is the scalar-current coalgebra.

It describes composition of inputs stacked at the same curve positions along a transverse line.

An ambient mapping coalgebra classifies transverse actions. Requiring the actor itself to factorize is an extra condition and can destroy the existence of a final action.

A twisted group algebra has basis ugu_g, indexed by a finite group, with product uguh=c(g,h)ughu_gu_h=c(g,h)u_{gh}. The cocycle identity makes this multiplication associative.

Its matrix-block sizes turn coherence equations into divisibility constraints on representation dimensions.

For finite abelian groups in characteristic zero, the commutator pairing controls the center and simple block dimensions.

twisting state

A twisting state is a degree-one state q∈V⊗Aq\in V\otimes A satisfying dq+12q(0)q+w∈T(V⊗A)dq+\tfrac12q_{(0)}q+w\in T(V\otimes A), where VV is a degree-zero vertex algebra and (A,d,w)(A,d,w) is a curved commutative vertex algebra. The coupling J⊗cJ\otimes c expresses the Heisenberg current and its curved ghost algebra through reciprocal universal properties.

This is a curved Maurer–Cartan equation modulo translation. A twisting state is different from a twisting cochain out of a coalgebra.

two-sided bar

The two-sided bar of a right A-module M and a left A-module N has terms consisting of M, a word of A entries, and N. Its differential combines internal differentials, adjacent multiplications and both endpoint actions. Its derived totalization computes the tensor of M and N over A.

Keeping both endpoints makes interface composition and the coring diagonal explicit.

Deconcatenation retains every cut, including the empty prefix and suffix. Omitting endpoint terms can destroy the chain identity and the unit for composition.

U

unipotent tensor category

A unipotent tensor category in this setting is a finite-length abelian tensor category whose only simple object is the unit. Every object is built by successive extensions of the unit.

Why it matters

Unit self-extensions then control the primitive part of the coefficient coalgebra and provide the spectral regularity test.

Where it sits

Exact tensor products make composition lengths multiplicative. Unipotence does not force the coefficient coalgebra to be cocommutative or translation to have only finite orbits.

universal R-matrix

A universal R-matrix is an invertible tensor for a Hopf algebra that intertwines the coproduct with its opposite and satisfies the two coproduct identities producing the tensor hexagons.

Why it matters

It supplies coherent exchange maps on representations of the Hopf algebra.

Where it sits

For an infinite algebra, the tensor, its inverse and every product in those identities must belong to a declared completed tensor domain.

Related

  • Hopf algebra

vacuum

A vacuum in a vertex algebra is a distinguished state 𝟏\mathbf1 satisfying Y(𝟏,z)=idY(\mathbf1,z)=\mathrm{id} and Y(a,z)𝟏=ezTaY(a,z)\mathbf1=e^{zT}a. It is the identity insertion and the state from which fields create translated states.

Why it matters

Singular products can have nonzero vacuum coefficients that must survive duality.

Where it sits

The local vacuum belongs to a nonempty insertion. A cut tensor has a separate unit at the empty configuration, and a prepared state is an evaluation of observables.

Vandermonde

The Vandermonde polynomial in roots x1,…,xnx_1,\ldots,x_n is ∏i<j(xj−xi)\prod_{i\lt j}(x_j-x_i). Its square is symmetric and vanishes where two roots coincide.

Why it matters

Multiplication by the squared Vandermonde gives the explicit comparison between the two even shuffle products.

Where it sits

Its factorization into within-block and cross-block factors proves compatibility in every charge. Inverting it removes the root-collision locus.

  • shuffle algebra

vanishing cycles

Vanishing cycles are sheaf-theoretic coefficients that measure the change between a singular fibre of a function and its nearby fibres. Their degree convention and monodromy are part of the construction.

Critical Hall operations must transport the coefficients of their actual potential.

Compactly supported dimensional reduction is a pushforward theorem; it does not identify every restricted vanishing-cycle sheaf with a constant sheaf.

  • critical locus

variational derivative

A variational derivative of a functional is the coefficient of a field variation after integration by parts. For local functionals it is generally a distribution. Odd field variations require a specified left or right derivative convention.

Why it matters

It determines the conjugate-field source and Hamiltonian action of a boundary observable.

Where it sits

A distributional variation need not be a smooth tangent vector before heat regularization.

Related

  • local functional

vector space

A vector space over a coefficient field is a collection whose elements can be added and multiplied by scalars, satisfying the linearity laws. A linear map preserves addition and scalar multiplication.

Why it matters

States, coefficients and infinitesimal variations begin as vector spaces before products and differentials are added.

Where it sits

A topology, grading or completion supplies additional structure and can change which linear maps are allowed.

Related

  • coefficient field

Verdier duality

Verdier duality is the geometric contravariant duality that exchanges direct-image and exceptional-extension operations. For bounded holonomic differential-module complexes it is involutive; an open immersion satisfies j!=𝔻j∗𝔻j_!=\mathbb D j_*\mathbb D on that domain.

Applied to a bar coalgebra, it produces an associative algebra for the convolution with dualized geometric functors.

It retains support information that an internal dual into the isolated empty unit would lose. Extending coefficient duality to full currents uses a separately specified pro-perfect category.

vertex algebra

A vertex algebra is a vector space VV with a vacuum 𝟏\mathbf1, translation TT, and fields Y(a,z)b∈V((z))Y(a,z)b\in V((z)). The vacuum creates translated states, translation differentiates fields, and locality and associativity compare their singular products. Locality means a sufficiently high power of z−wz-w kills the field commutator, with the parity sign for odd states.

Why it matters

It records all coefficients of local field products, not only a mode Lie bracket.

Heisenberg and affine current algebras provide examples. Quantum vertex algebras retain a specified exchange operator.

vertex coalgebra

A vertex coalgebra has a counit, a translation operator and mode coproducts satisfying the identities dual to those of a vertex algebra. A graded continuous dual gives such a structure when every transposed mode lands in the declared tensor product.

It retains the regular and singular coefficients of the completed fields under duality.

Its mode coproducts differ from deconcatenation in an associative bar. The continuous dual here has finite weight and finite character-jet support.

vertex ideal

A vertex ideal is a submodule stable under all left and right field modes and the required translation operators.

Why it matters

It permits full fields and vacuum data to descend to a quotient.

Where it sits

A scalar relation passing only a first-derivative test need not generate a proper vertex ideal.

Related

W

wave operator

A wave operator is a strong limit comparing two unitary evolutions at large positive or negative time on their absolutely continuous subspaces.

Why it matters

Its ranges determine whether scattering is complete.

Where it sits

Unitary scattering does not imply positivity of the associated trace distribution.

  • spectral shift

Weil form

The Weil form is qW(f,g)=W(f∗g∗)q_W(f,g)=W(f*g^*), where WW is the complete signed explicit-formula functional.

Its positivity on every compact complex test is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis.

Both polar terms, the gamma contribution and every prime power must remain. Positivity on a restricted domain needs an explicit extension argument.

A Weyl algebra is generated by coordinate and momentum symbols with relations [xi,pj]=ℏδij[x_i,p_j]=\hbar\delta_{ij}, while coordinates commute among themselves and momenta commute among themselves.

It gives the even quantum coefficient algebra and the operators on Fock space.

The choice of polynomial or completed coefficients affects its modules and possible augmentations.

A Wick contraction pairs two field slots using a chosen two-point kernel and removes those slots. Summing over pairings, with the graded signs and factorials, defines the corresponding quantum product.

Why it matters

Contractions give explicit formulas for current products and transport between heat scales.

Connected contraction graphs give the Taylor coefficients of logarithmic, or connected, expectations. Disjoint supports can make a singular propagator smooth on every paired input.

word truncation

The word truncation of a tensor algebra T(M) at length L is its quotient by the ideal generated by all words of length at least L. Products whose total length reaches L become zero.

Why it matters

It gives explicit quotient algebras for studying the derived coring and its nonsplit two-sided extension.

Reconstruction from successive derived truncations is proved on modules bounded below in word weight. A Laurent module with weights unbounded below can be invisible to every chosen truncation.

Word weight is the grading that assigns weight one to each tensor generator and adds weights under concatenation. A module is bounded below in this grading if all components below one fixed integer vanish.

Why it matters

In a reconstruction tower, the error at stage r starts at increasingly large word weight. A lower bound on the module makes that error vanish at each fixed weight.

Word weight is separate from cohomological degree and from the number of geometric positions. Each supplies a different finiteness condition.

The Wess–Zumino–Witten vacuum is the distinguished vacuum representation of the chiral current algebra in the WZW model at its specified group and level.

It is a candidate description of a full boundary state space in the appropriate gauge-theory regime.

Where it sits

The allowed level and nonperturbative sectors matter. A positive-level identification does not determine a degenerate level-zero boundary algebra.

Related

  • vacuum

Three insertions must have a consistent total exchange.
